body: I am not sure what the protocol is here, but I am happy to also add `get_value_at_index` since it fits the theme of this PR and would require practically no additional work. But I didn't do it because my proposal didn't propose it.
Given that `Dictionary` already has `keys()` and `values()` methods, I find it logical and consistent if we also had `key(i)` and `value(i)` methods.

I agree this function totally makes sense for an ordered dictionary.

I do have some reservation though at the current state of `Dictionary`'s implementation, because `get_key_at_index` is a deceptively slow method. This is because `Dictionary` is linked list based. On every call of `get_key_at_index` it iterates the dictionary, which is especially slow in linked lists because of cache misses.

Users might be incentivised to iterate a dictionary with `int` values like so:
```
for i in dict.size():
    var key := dict.get_key_at_index(i)
    var value := dict.get_value_at_index(i)
```
Since this is now creating one visible outer loop and one visible inner loop, it would be an `O(n log n)` operation, and would be unexpectedly slow for users.
This problem does not exist for `keys()` and `values()` because the dictionary is iterated only once for those methods, staying at `O(n)`.

Arguably, the better solution to this problem would be to start using an array based hash map, but we have no suitable candidate for that right now (`AHashMap` does not guarantee insertion order right now, at least on erase).

If we agree this function is needed, I think we should
- Improve `get_key_at_index` to make bounds checks before iterating the dictionary.
- Improve `get_key_at_index` to iterate the dictionary backwards when the index is nearer to the back.
- Document that this function will iterate the dictionary and can be unexpectedly slow.
- Possibly start looking into a list based `Dictionary` implementation.
closes https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/11447, or at least satisfies my use-case.

> * Improve `get_key_at_index` to iterate the dictionary backwards when the index is nearer to the back.

This is odd indeed!
I do have one guess: Did you happen to benchmark only one call of `get_key_at_index` (instead of, say, 10000 calls)? If so, the discrepancy might be because the back of the dictionary is still in RAM cache, while the front has been wiped from it by the time you call `get_key_at_index`.

> I do have one guess: Did you happen to benchmark only one call of `get_key_at_index` (instead of, say, 10000 calls)?

I originally benchmarked this poorly by simply calling it once per frame in a simple scene and using the in-Editor profiler. I wrote a better benchmarking script and the discrepancy disappears:

```
Dictionary Size: 100000
-----------------------
Running .get_key_at_index() 10000 times:
    Index 0 took 2.076 ms
    Index 10 took 2.302 ms
    Index 100 took 4.509 ms
    Index 1000 took 33.017 ms

    Index 99999 took 2.192 ms
    Index 99989 took 2.345 ms
    Index 99899 took 4.505 ms
    Index 98999 took 32.537 ms

```

Near the ends of the dictionary, the execution times are largely dominated by overhead. Most applications for index-based key retrieval only target these areas. I've never seen an application for retrieving the key in the middle of a dictionary, so I don't think this is a problem.

I should also mention that this is also faster than the previous implementation of this method which iterated through the HashMap object and had a conditional inside the loop.

Hi @theXYZT, sorry for getting back to you so late.

The idea of exposing `get_key_at_index` was discussed among maintainers. Most prominently, people were concerned about potential misuse of this function (by iterating `dictionary.size()` and then using `dictionary.get_key_at_index` in the loop; the same performance footgun brought up above). We've actually found that most in-engine uses of the function fell into that exact trap 😅 (addressed by the issue I just linked, #104082). 
As such, there is hesitation around merging the function, to avoid people footgunning themselves in the same way. We may even consider removing `get_key_at_index` from `Dictionary` in-engine, to avoid similar problems in the future.

I understand your main use-case is getting the first item of the dictionary, which in itself doesn't have the same performance limitation. Perhaps something like `get_first_key()` and `get_first_value()` would be less problematic for reviewers? It's at least worth exploring this option.
I also see a GDExtension being able to solve this (though that would be a lot more work to set up).

As far as I know, other languages also don't offer index-based retrieval functions. IIRC, in Python, the answer is usually `next(iter(ordered_dict.keys()))` — which unfortunately doesn't work for us because Godot `keys()` returns an array, not some kind of iterator.

I'm sorry, I wish I could give you a nice and simple solution!
Let me know your thoughts, I'm happy to continue to work with you to find a fitting solution!

In my opinion, GDScript currently lacks some nice performant data structures that can be very helpful for developers. The current implementation of `Dictionary` provides two neat functions:

1. Insertion order guarantee -- this is very useful for various forms of LRU caches or time-based caches.

2. A performant deque-like structure -- Being based on a doubly-linked list, just allowing access to the first and last elements can enable users to get more value out of `Dictionary` as a data structure. A queue is obviously useful in a significant number of algorithms.  Currently, there is no performant way of implementing FIFO logic using existing Variants, since popping from the front of Arrays is quite slow.

For both of these, something simple like `.first()` and `.last()` would easily suffice.

---

I previously liked the `.get_key_at_index()` method because it provides a fast way of getting ANY element by index, instead of limiting the user to only the first and last element. I didn't see any good reason why the user needs to be prevented from doing this, and I didn't think that `.get_key_at_index()` would be a "footgun" if appropriately documented. Also, since this is my first PR, I was trying to use existing methods without changing too much as I thought that would be preferred to suggesting new methods.

That being said, anyone who has a clever use for `.get_key_at_index()` is probably not averse to writing their own GDExtension or just building their own fork of the engine. Working on this PR gave me the confidence to do just that!

Additionally, I want to point out that the first comment on the `Dictionary` docs page is about implementing a `.pick_random()` (a method I've seen requested multiple times elsewhere too) which is very easy to implement using a `.get_key_at_index()` method.

---

So, I think my revised proposal is:

1. `.first()` and `.last()` methods for `Dictionary` which return the keys for the first and last element respectively.

2. Optionally, a `.pick_random()` method that returns a random key and uses the underlying `.get_key_at_index()` method to do so.

3. Keep the optimizations in this PR to `.get_key_at_index()` and associated methods and not remove them from the C++ code for anyone who might want to write interesting GDExtension code using them.

If preferred, I am happy to open a new PR for points 1 and 2 and restrict this PR to the changes in point 3 only. What do you think?

> In my opinion, GDScript currently lacks some nice performant data structures that can be very helpful for developers. The current implementation of Dictionary provides two neat functions:

Agreed. I think this is mostly down to `Variant` types being difficult to add :)

> A performant deque-like structure -- Being based on a doubly-linked list, just allowing access to the first and last elements can enable users to get more value out of Dictionary as a data structure. A queue is obviously useful in a significant number of algorithms. Currently, there is no performant way of implementing FIFO logic using existing Variants, since popping from the front of Arrays is quite slow.

Side note, linked lists aren't very well suited for Deques. Ringbuffers almost always perform better, and could already be implemented with a wrapper over `Array` (though I'm not sure if, through GDScript overhead, `Dictionary` wouldn't be faster still practically). 

> I didn't see any good reason why the user needs to be prevented from doing this, and I didn't think that .get_key_at_index() would be a "footgun" if appropriately documented. 

During the maintainers' discussion, it was mentioned that while documentation can be great at explanation _how_ something works, notes on where _not_ to use it will rarely be noticed. The only way to ensure it isn't used in a loop would probably be to call it something like `get_key_at_index_do_not_use_in_a_loop` :)

> That being said, anyone who has a clever use for .get_key_at_index() is probably not averse to writing their own GDExtension or just building their own fork of the engine. Working on this PR gave me the confidence to do just that!

Yes, this would definitely be possible with a GDExtension!

> .first() and .last() methods for Dictionary which return the keys for the first and last element respectively.

Sounds good to me (though I don't speak for all maintainers).
My main gripe with these would be that they're very 'narrow' in usefulness, but at least there's no footguns involved. The best way to solve your problem would probably be finding something that doesn't require exposing a new function, but unfortunately I can't think of anything.

> Optionally, a .pick_random() method that returns a random key and uses the underlying .get_key_at_index() method to do so.

I'm less sold on this one, at the very least it should probably be a different PR.

> Keep the optimizations in this PR to .get_key_at_index() and associated methods and not remove them from the C++ code for anyone who might want to write interesting GDExtension code using them.

I was looking at `get_key_at_index` callers, hoping to remove it fully, but it seems some of its callers _are_ actually somewhat legitimate. So I wouldn't mind merging a performance improvement. I'd probably pack that into a new PR though, as this one has gotten quite a lot of feedback that would be unrelated to the new use-case.
